Patients with HIV infection and AIDS are at in- creased risk of specific bacterial, fungal, protozoal, and vi- ral infections largely as a result of impaired cell-mediated immunity. With the introduction of antimicrobial prophy- laxis and HAART there has been a significant decrease in the incidence of most AIDS-defining opportunistic infec- tions, especially in the developed world. However, HIV- related opportunistic infections and deaths still occur in pa- tients newly diagnosed with HIV infection, in those in the early course of HAART, in those non-adherent to their HIV treatment, or in those with drug-resistant HIV infec- tion; deaths also result from non-opportunistic infections and chronic viral hepatitis.1 • Infections affecting the lungs include recurrent bacterial pneumonia (p.186), pneumocystis pneumonia (p.521), and pulmonary tuberculosis (p.196). • Many pathogens cause gastrointestinal-tract disease in HIV-infected patients, including candida oesophagitis (p.518), CMV colitis (p.853), and amoebiasis (p.822), cryptosporidiosis (p.
